title: Problem Overview: Unavoidable Cycle Lengths
content: Erdős Problem #72 ($100 prize) asks: does there exist a set A of natural numbers with density 0 and a constant c > 0 such that every sufficiently large graph with average degree ≥ c contains a cycle whose length is in A? The answer is YES, proved non-constructively by Verstraëte (2005) and constructively for powers of 2 by Liu-Montgomery (2020), contradicting Erdős's intuition.
mathContext: $\exists A \subseteq \mathbb{N}, \text{dens}(A) = 0, \exists c > 0, \forall G \text{ large with } \bar{d}(G) \geq c, \exists k \in A, C_k \subseteq G$. Here $\text{dens}(A) = \lim_{n \to \infty} |A \cap [1,n]|/n$ and $\bar{d}(G) = 2|E|/|V|$.

title: Counting Function and Density Zero
content: The counting function |A ∩ [0,n]| counts elements of A up to n, implemented as Finset.filter over Finset.range. A set has density 0 if this count divided by n tends to 0, formalized via Tendsto to nhds 0. Powers of 2 have counting function ~log₂(n), while arithmetic progressions grow linearly.
mathContext: $\text{countingFunction}(A, n) = |\{a \in A : a \leq n\}|$. $\text{hasDensityZero}(A) := \text{countingFunction}(A, n)/n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. For powers of 2: $|\{2^k : 2^k \leq n\}| = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1 = O(\log n)$, so density is $O(\log n / n) \to 0$.

title: Powers of Two: The Key Set
content: The set {2^k : k ∈ ℕ} = {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...} is defined as a Set ℕ via existential quantification. Erdős believed this set would NOT work as an unavoidable cycle length set, but Liu-Montgomery proved it does. The density zero proof (sorry) follows from the counting function being O(log n).
mathContext: $\text{powersOfTwo} = \{n \in \mathbb{N} : \exists k, n = 2^k\}$. Only $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ elements lie in $[1,n]$, giving density $O(\log n / n) \to 0$.

title: Arithmetic Progressions: Positive Density Contrast
content: Arithmetic progressions {a + kd : k ∈ ℕ} have density 1/d > 0, so they cannot solve the density-0 version of the problem. However, Bollobás (1977) proved they are unavoidable when they contain even numbers, demonstrating the cycle-forcing phenomenon exists.
mathContext: $\text{AP}(a, d) = \{a + kd : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ has $|\text{AP}(a,d) \cap [1,n]| \sim n/d$, so $\text{dens}(\text{AP}(a,d)) = 1/d > 0$. The theorem `arithmeticProgression_positive_density` (sorry) states $\neg\text{hasDensityZero}(\text{AP}(a,d))$.

title: Graph Definitions: Average Degree and Cycle Lengths
content: Three key definitions: (1) averageDegree = (Σ deg(v))/|V| = 2|E|/|V|; (2) cycleLengths = set of k such that G contains a k-cycle, using SimpleGraph.Walk.IsCycle; (3) containsCycleIn checks whether cycleLengths intersects a target set A. These build on Mathlib's SimpleGraph infrastructure.
mathContext: $\bar{d}(G) = \frac{1}{|V|} \sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = \frac{2|E|}{|V|}$. $\text{cycleLengths}(G) = \{k : \exists \text{ cycle of length } k \text{ in } G\}$. Uses `SimpleGraph.Walk` for paths and `Walk.IsCycle` for the cycle predicate.

title: Unavoidable and Strongly Unavoidable Sets
content: A set A is unavoidable with threshold c if every graph on ≥ n₀ vertices with average degree ≥ c contains a cycle of length in A. It is strongly unavoidable if some such c exists. The existential quantifier over n₀ allows excluding small graphs where the property may fail trivially.
mathContext: $\text{isUnavoidable}(A, c) := \exists n_0, \forall G \text{ on } \geq n_0 \text{ vertices}, \bar{d}(G) \geq c \Rightarrow \text{cycleLengths}(G) \cap A \neq \emptyset$. $\text{isStronglyUnavoidable}(A) := \exists c > 0, \text{isUnavoidable}(A, c)$. The crucial point: $c$ is independent of $|V|$.

title: Erdős Problem #72: Formal Statement
content: The formal problem: does there exist a density-0 set A that is strongly unavoidable? This combines number-theoretic sparsity (density 0) with extremal graph theory (cycle forcing by average degree). Defined as Erdos72Statement, it is proved by erdos_72_solved using Liu-Montgomery.

title: Bollobás (1977): Arithmetic Progressions
content: Bollobás proved that infinite arithmetic progressions containing even numbers are strongly unavoidable. While this doesn't solve Problem #72 (APs have positive density), it establishes the cycle-forcing phenomenon. The requirement of even numbers connects to the bipartite structure: odd cycles are harder to force.
mathContext: If $\text{AP}(a,d)$ contains an even number (i.e., $\exists k, 2 \mid (a + kd)$), then $\text{isStronglyUnavoidable}(\text{AP}(a,d))$. The even condition is necessary: the set $\{1, 3, 5, 7, \ldots\}$ is not unavoidable since bipartite graphs have no odd cycles regardless of density.

title: Verstraëte (2005): Non-Constructive Existence
content: Verstraëte proved non-constructively that some density-0 set is strongly unavoidable, solving Problem #72 in principle. The proof uses probabilistic and compactness arguments, establishing existence without identifying which specific sets work. This left open the constructive question answered by Liu-Montgomery.
mathContext: `verstraete_existence : Erdos72Statement` — a pure existence axiom. The proof in [Ve05] uses probabilistic methods to show a random sparse subset of even numbers is unavoidable with high probability.

title: Liu-Montgomery (2020): Powers of 2 Work
content: The breakthrough result: powers of 2 are strongly unavoidable. There exists a constant c > 0 such that every sufficiently large graph with average degree ≥ c contains a cycle whose length is a power of 2. Combined with density-zero of powers of 2, this yields the constructive solution erdos_72_solved.
mathContext: `liu_montgomery_powers_of_two : isStronglyUnavoidable powersOfTwo`. Combined with `powersOfTwo_density_zero`, yields `erdos_72_solved : Erdos72Statement` via `⟨powersOfTwo, powersOfTwo_density_zero, liu_montgomery_powers_of_two⟩`.

title: Erdős Was Wrong: Refuted Belief
content: Erdős stated he was 'almost certain' that powers of 2 would NOT be unavoidable, expecting the required threshold to grow with graph size. The theorem erdos_was_wrong formally refutes this: since liu_montgomery_powers_of_two proves isStronglyUnavoidable powersOfTwo, the negation ¬isStronglyUnavoidable powersOfTwo is false.
mathContext: `erdos_incorrect_belief := ¬isStronglyUnavoidable powersOfTwo`. `erdos_was_wrong : ¬erdos_incorrect_belief` follows by applying `liu_montgomery_powers_of_two` to the hypothesis. This is a rare instance of Erdős's combinatorial intuition being definitively wrong.

title: Other Density-0 Sets and Open Questions
content: Perfect squares {k² : k ∈ ℕ} have density 0 (~√n/n → 0), but whether they are strongly unavoidable remains open. The theorem powersOfTwo_all_even shows that powers of 2 are all even (except 1), which is key to the Liu-Montgomery argument — bipartite graphs exclude odd cycles, so even-length cycles are the right target.
mathContext: $\text{perfectSquares} = \{k^2 : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ with $|\text{perfectSquares} \cap [1,n]| = \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor$, so $\text{dens} = O(n^{-1/2}) \to 0$. The evenness property: $2^k$ is even for $k \geq 1$, proved by `⟨2^{k-1}, \text{ring}⟩$ in the successor case.

title: Optimal Threshold and Explicit Bounds
content: The optimal threshold for a set A is the infimum of all c > 0 for which A is unavoidable. Liu-Montgomery gives an explicit but large bound (< 10^6) for powers of 2. Finding the true optimal threshold remains open — it may be much smaller, perhaps even a small constant.
mathContext: $\text{optimalThreshold}(A) = \inf\{c > 0 : \text{isUnavoidable}(A, c)\}$. Liu-Montgomery: $\text{optimalThreshold}(\text{powersOfTwo}) < 10^6$. The true value is conjectured to be much smaller.

title: General Liu-Montgomery Theorem
content: Liu-Montgomery actually proved a more general result: any set A with logarithmic growth (|A ∩ [1,n]| ≤ log₂(n) + 1) consisting of even numbers (plus possibly 1) is strongly unavoidable. Powers of 2 is a special case. This characterizes a broad class of unavoidable sets.
mathContext: If $|A \cap [1,n]| \leq \log_2(n) + 1$ and $\forall a \in A, 2 \mid a \text{ or } a = 1$, then $\text{isStronglyUnavoidable}(A)$. This uses `hasControlledGrowth A (fun n => Nat.log 2 n + 1)` for the growth bound.
